explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, “…the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.” Not just the people. Verse 4 says the seventh year is “…a Sabbath of complete rest for the land…” and that's a whole year off. I know folks who can't rest half as well as a field can.
I get the thinking, since a house is a nice place to put your feet up. But the verse says the land itself must observe the Sabbath. Houses show up later in the chapter, and they get their own rules.

A resting shovel sounds lovely, and I bet my stamper handle would sign up fast. But God doesn't name the tools. He says, “…the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.” What He rules out in that seventh year is sowing the field and pruning the vineyard (Leviticus 25:4).

Not this time, friend. God says, “You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines.” That's the Sabbath year. The land must have a year of complete rest.

Right. In the Sabbath year, God says, “You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines.” The land must have a year of complete rest. So the vines get left alone, and that's the whole point.

explanations.answer: The household and even the wild animals
explanations.explanation: Yes! The food is for you, your manservant and maidservant, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you, your livestock and the wild animals in your land. That's a wide table. Even the critters get a seat, and they didn't have to bring a dish.

explanations.answer: The widows and orphans of the town
explanations.explanation: Good heart on that guess, but these verses don't name widows or orphans. They list your household, the hired hand or foreigner staying with you, your livestock and the wild animals. Then verse 7 says, “All its growth may serve as food.”

These verses don't list priests or Levites here. Instead they name the household, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you, the livestock and the wild animals. That's a surprisingly long guest list for a year with no sowing.

God says to sound the horn “…on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement.” (Leviticus 25:9) Seven times seven years, forty-nine of them, and then THE HORN. I think that's the loudest alarm clock anybody ever got, and nobody's hitting snooze on it. It goes “…far and wide…” and it's the signal for the fiftieth year, the Jubilee.
Passover is a big day, but it isn't the one named here. God says the horn sounds on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. The horn goes out far and wide on that day.

The Feast of Tabernacles is a fun one, and I see why it popped into your head. But this verse names a different day. The horn is sounded on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. God says to sound it throughout the land.

explanations.answer: Back to his own property and clan
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “…each of you is to return to his property and to his clan.” Then verse 13 says it again, that each shall return to his own property. Liberty means going home.

explanations.answer: Up to the place God will choose
explanations.explanation: This passage doesn't say anything like that for the Jubilee. God says each person is to return to his property and to his clan. The direction is home, not up.

explanations.answer: Out to the fields to glean
explanations.explanation: Gleaning is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't what God says for liberty. The instruction is that each of you is to return to his property and to his clan. About the fields in that year, God says, “you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” So the fields rest while the people head home.

Yes! God says, “The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” (Leviticus 25:11) So the land rests in the seventh year and rests again in the fiftieth. Plenty of time to put its feet up.

It's true, friend, and it's an easy one to second-guess. God says, “The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” (Leviticus 25:11) The land rests then too, even though it already rests every seventh year.

Yes. More years before the Jubilee means more harvests to sell, so God says you “…shall increase the price in proportion to a greater number of years…” The buyer gets more harvests, so he pays more. It's like a big batch of cookies costing more than a half dozen.

Right. Fewer years left means fewer harvests, so God says to “…decrease it in proportion to a lesser number of years…” Then He gives the reason: “for he is selling you a given number of harvests.” So the buyer pays for the harvests that are left.
A fixed price would be easy, but the price moves with the years. God says to increase it for a greater number of years and decrease it for a lesser number. The count changes the price.
Nothing here is left to luck. God says to buy “…according to the number of years since the last Jubilee…” and the seller sells according to the harvest years remaining. The price follows the count.

Hidden doesn't fit, baker. Both sides count the years since the last Jubilee and the harvest years remaining, and the price follows that count. God also says, “Do not take advantage of each other…” (Leviticus 25:17). A price set by a count of years is the opposite of a mystery.

explanations.answer: They will dwell securely in the land
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says to keep His statutes and carefully observe His judgments “…so that you may dwell securely in the land.” Verse 19 adds that they can eat their fill and dwell in safety. Security and a full belly, that's what He says follows.

explanations.answer: They will rule over the nations nearby
explanations.explanation: Ruling the neighbors is a big promise, but it isn't what God says here. He says keeping His statutes and judgments means they “…may dwell securely in the land.” Security is the promise.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will make peace with them
explanations.explanation: These verses don't mention enemies at all. God says keeping His statutes and judgments is “…so that you may dwell securely in the land.” Then the land yields its fruit and they dwell in safety.

explanations.answer: Yields a crop for three years
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says, “But I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year, so that the land will yield a crop sufficient for three years.” That answers the worry about what they'd eat in the seventh year. God answers their question before they even have to ask it twice.

explanations.answer: Yields only enough for one year
explanations.explanation: One year's worth wouldn't carry them through a year of rest, and that isn't what God says. He says the land will yield “…a crop sufficient for three years.” That's His blessing in the sixth year.
The verse doesn't split it up like that. God says His blessing in the sixth year means the land will yield “…a crop sufficient for three years.” It's one blessing, and it's big.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of it. God says, “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.” It's His land, so nobody sells it for good.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the priests
explanations.explanation: The priests aren't named as owners here. God says the land can't be sold permanently “…because it is Mine…” He's the owner, and the Israelites are foreigners and residents with Him.

explanations.answer: Because the land belongs to the king
explanations.explanation: No king is mentioned in this passage. God says the land can't be sold permanently “…because it is Mine…” The deed is His. And He calls the Israelites “…foreigners and residents with Me.”

Right. God says, “…his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.” Notice the word may, so the door is open for a close relative to step in. Having someone like that around is a gift.

I get it, baker, a high priest sounds like a very official person to call. But the text sends a different way: “…his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.” (Leviticus 25:25) It's family stepping up. Think of the relative who shows up with a truck when you're moving, only this one shows up with the money.

Elders are a fair guess, baker. But the verse puts it on family: “…his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.” (Leviticus 25:25) The elders aren't named in these verses at all. The one stepping in is a close relative.

Yes. God says, “…he shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property.” It's a count of years, and then home he goes. Years are what this whole chapter counts, from the Sabbath year to the Jubilee.

Tithes are a good guess, friend, but they don't show up in these verses. The man “…shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property.” (Leviticus 25:27) Count the years, pay what's left, and he walks back onto his land. Nobody has to bring a calculator the size of my oven.
Feasts would make for a fun calculation, but that isn't what God says. The man calculates the years since the sale and repays the balance. Then he returns to his property.

Not quite, friend. God says that if he can't obtain enough to repay, what he sold stays with the buyer “…until the Year of Jubilee.” Then it says, “In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.” It doesn't stay forever.

That's right. If he can't get enough to repay, the land stays with the buyer only until the Year of Jubilee. Then God says, “In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.” So the sale has an end date built in.

explanations.answer: Help him so he can keep living among them
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! God says to help him “…as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” (Leviticus 25:35) The goal is that he keeps living right there with his people. I think that means the help is meant to come while he's still standing in the neighborhood, not after. The command is simple: help him.

explanations.answer: Send him to the priests to be cared for
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. God tells the people, “…you are to help him…” so that he can continue to live among you. The help comes from the neighbors.

explanations.answer: Leave his own clan to deal with him
explanations.explanation: Leaving it to his clan is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't what God says. He tells the people, “…you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” The word is help, and the people hearing it are the ones He's talking to. Nobody gets to wave this one off and hope for the best.

That's right. God says, “Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you.” No interest, no profit. The goal is that he can keep living among them.
A cloak isn't mentioned in this passage. What God says not to take is “…any interest or profit…” That's the instruction for helping a destitute countryman.

A tenth of his harvest is a fair guess, but the passage never brings it up here. God says, “Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you.” That's the thing He rules out. The point is that a man in need can keep living among them.

explanations.answer: As a hired worker and not a slave
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “…you must not force him into slave labor.” Instead he stays “…as a hired worker or temporary resident…” and works for the buyer until the Year of Jubilee. That's a hired worker's arrangement, not a slave's.

explanations.answer: As a slave for the rest of his life
explanations.explanation: That isn't what God says for a countryman. He says, “…you must not force him into slave labor.” and the man works only until the Year of Jubilee. Verse 46 says no man may rule harshly over his brother, the Israelites.

explanations.answer: As a prisoner until he pays up
explanations.explanation: A prisoner isn't in the picture, baker. God says the man stays as a hired worker or temporary resident, and he works until the Year of Jubilee. Nothing in these verses calls him a prisoner. It describes a worker with an end date.

Yes! God says, “Then he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” The Year of Jubilee frees the man and his children. And the way back to his clan and his fathers' property is open to him.

It's true, baker. In the Year of Jubilee, “…he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” (Leviticus 25:41) The Jubilee frees him and his children. And the way home to his clan is open.

explanations.answer: They're His servants He brought out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves.” Their belonging starts with Him. Verse 55 says it again: “For the Israelites are My servants.”

explanations.answer: There are too few of them to spare
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about their numbers. God's reason is, “…the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt…” That's why they are not to be sold as slaves.

explanations.answer: Their fathers made a vow at Sinai
explanations.explanation: A vow at Sinai is a fair guess, since Moses is on Mount Sinai when this chapter opens (Leviticus 25:1). But no vow is named in these verses. God gives His own reason: He brought them out of the land of Egypt, and they are His servants. That's why none of them is to be sold as slaves.

Not here, friend. God says, “…as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” (Leviticus 25:46) He says it again in verse 43: “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.”

That's right. God says, “…as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” (Leviticus 25:46) He says the same in verse 43: “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.” So under these rules, harshness toward a fellow Israelite is ruled out in both places.

Yes. The word in the text is redeem, and here it means someone pays the price to buy him back. God says one of his brothers may redeem him, and then lists his uncle, his cousin or any close relative from his clan. If he prospers, he may even redeem himself.
Being sent back is a nice thought, but the text says he can be redeemed. A price is figured in verses 50 to 52, so the word is bought back. His uncle, cousin or any close relative may do it.
Being called back sounds friendly, but the text says redeemed. A price is worked out based on the years left until the Jubilee. That means bought back.

Not quite, baker. Look at what God says: “Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) So if nobody buys him back, the Jubilee releases him, and his children go with him. He doesn't stay with that owner for life.

Right. Even if nobody buys him back, God says, “…he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) The Jubilee frees him, and his children go free with him. Redemption is one way out, and the Jubilee is there even without it.
